title: instant karma?
hook: the vending machine tips over, everyone says karma: what the Buddha actually meant
carry: I am the owner of my actions

segments.voice: Instant karma. A man kicks a vending machine and it tips over onto him. Someone cuts the line and their coffee comes out wrong. Everyone in the comments reaches for the same word, and they mean payback: the universe as a referee, settling scores where you can watch. It's satisfying. It's also not what the Buddha meant, and his version points the other way: back at the one acting. First, a guess.

Karma, or kamma in Pali, means action. A deed. Something done. Then the Buddha sharpened it. In one discourse he says it plainly: intention is what I call karma. Before the hand moves or the words come out, there's a leaning, a choice. That's where it starts. And then it grows. The old texts use a farming picture: deeds are seeds, and their results ripen like fruit. Not because a judge is keeping score. Because that's what seeds do. Two surprises. First, it's mostly about the one acting. Every choice shapes the chooser: patience, practiced, makes a patient person. Second, not everything is karma. Asked whether everything a person feels comes from past deeds, the Buddha said no: illness, weather, accidents and other people's choices play their part. So 'they deserved it' was never the point. In many temples and monasteries, people chant a reflection on it: I am the owner of my actions, heir to my actions.
screen: `KARMA — ACTION` · `INTENTION IS KARMA` · `SEEDS, THEN FRUIT` · `NOT EVERYTHING IS KARMA` · then, large: `I AM THE OWNER OF MY ACTIONS.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Bring to mind the next thing you'll do: a message, a meeting, a meal. Breathe in, and notice the intention underneath it. Breathe out, and let it lean toward kindness, if you like. That leaning is where karma starts.
Karma. Action, and the intention inside it: what you mean, and what it grows. First word on your strand.

howItsDone: Buddhists understand karma as intentional action and what it ripens into; in many temples and monasteries a daily reflection is chanted that ends 'I am the owner of my actions, heir to my actions', and people try to act from kind intentions in ordinary life.

fork.setup: a man asks the Buddha: is everything a person feels caused by their own past deeds? what does the Buddha answer?
options: no: illness, weather and accidents play a part too.
fork.reveal: he says no, and lists other causes, from illness to the seasons to accidents. karma is real, but it isn't everything.

trapdoor: what you thought: the universe paying people back.
what it means: intentional action, and what it grows in the one who acts.
what a scholar hears: kamma, action. 'intention, I tell you, is kamma' (AN 6.63); results are vipāka, ripening; and SN 36.21 denies that everything felt comes from past kamma.

story.title: the insult nobody took
story.text: A furious man storms up to the Buddha and insults him to his face, again and again. The Buddha waits until he's finished. Then he asks: when guests come to your house and don't eat the food you offer, whose food is it? Mine, the man says. Then this abuse is yours too, the Buddha says: I don't accept it. The story says the man was so struck that he asked to become a monk himself.

wrong.myth: karma means the universe pays people back.
wrong.truth: karma means action. the Buddha said intention is karma: what you mean and do, and what that grows.

sources.ref: Nibbedhika Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 6.63): intention is kamma
Samuddaka Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 11.10): as the seed is sown, so is the fruit
Sivaka Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 36.21): not all that is felt comes from past kamma
Upajjhatthana Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 5.57): the five reflections, 'owner of my actions, heir to my actions'

notes: New lesson, written 2026-10-06 for the rebuilt week one (audience research: karma is the single most-corrected idea, so it opens the path). Replaces metta, which moved to day 15.
'Intention is what I call karma' paraphrases AN 6.63 (cetanaham, bhikkhave, kammam vadami). Confirm.
The seed-and-fruit picture is cited to SN 11.10; the image is common across the discourses. Confirm a fitting reference.

SN 36.21 (Sivaka): the Buddha lists bile, phlegm, wind, their combination, change of seasons, careless behavior, assault and kamma as sources of feeling; the script simplifies to 'illness, weather, accidents and other people's choices'. Confirm the simplification is fair.

The five reflections (AN 5.57) are chanted daily in many Theravada monasteries and in Plum Village; the script says 'in many temples and monasteries'. 'I am the owner of my actions, heir to my actions' is the script's own rendering, not a quoted translation. Confirm.
Akkosa Sutta (SN 7.2): Akkosaka Bharadvaja abuses the Buddha; the guest-and-food question; he later goes forth. Told as a story; confirm the telling.
Schools differ on how karma ripens across lives; the script stays with what the schools share (intention, ripening, not everything is karma) and leaves rebirth to day 7.
